reasoning: A natural phrase for an experience from life. Both feminine endings are pronounced e, and حياتية has doubled y.
A courtesy response expressing willing agreement. Both tikrami and the suffix -ik address a woman; عين has long ee.

vowelled_arabic: لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهْ
meaning_fix: There is no might or power except through God.
reasoning: This everyday religious formula preserves its conventional recited endings and q pronunciation. بالله means through God, rather than simply God's.
The feminine addressee is indicated by final -i in بتلاقي, and ق is glottalized. Literally, you do not find work; inability to find it is a natural contextual reading.
The farewell reading selects the first-person verb, with ba-. The object suffix -ik addresses a woman.
A colloquial t-form meaning that something became damaged or stopped working. The ر is doubled.
A blessing meaning may God light your path. The bare verb expresses a wish, and -ak addresses a man.
This is an ordinary workplace and political vocabulary item. Conversational ق can be glottalized here, while a more formal news-register pronunciation retains q.
Common for exploiting a person or making use of an opportunity or resource. Final ل is doubled.
العجل is the tire in this context, and فقع means burst or popped. A flat tire need not have burst, so the English is too general.
The colloquial drink name commonly has د in place of ذ. More careful pronunciations can retain dh, and the initial vowel can be reduced.

meaning_fix: It isn't sinking in / I can't get my head around it.
reasoning: This is a feminine participle with the attached -li, figuratively describing an idea not getting through. It concerns comprehension or acceptance, not necessarily an inability to cope.
A familiar fixed hedge meaning I think or as far as I believe. The bare first-person verb belongs to this conventional expression; the realization of ظ is register-sensitive.
The ordinary Palestinian verb for remaining or continuing. ض is emphatic, and ل is doubled; kept applies when followed by another action.
It describes rash or dangerously impulsive behavior, rather than ordinary inattentive carelessness. The hyphen separates t and h so they are not read as th.
The pool or pond reading selects birke. This differs from barake, meaning blessing.
The initial vowel is colloquial ee rather than formal ay, and ط is emphatic. The word can denote a veterinarian, especially as shorthand for دكتور بيطري.
A past-tense verb meaning he whispered. It is understood and used in Palestinian speech, without the MSA final vowel.
The spoken vowels are oo in موسم and ee in زيتون. The article assimilates to ز, and the phrase normally refers to the olive harvest season.
In the ordinary urban pronunciation of this noun, ث becomes s. It commonly denotes an accident, particularly a traffic accident.
A natural conversational way to say this morning. The article assimilates to emphatic ص, and الصبح has a common spoken vowel between ب and ح.
Figuratively, this means going deeply into a subject, so detailed discussion is a natural contextual reading. It can also be literal; ق in عميق is glottalized.
سخونية is a colloquial term for fever. The initial short vowel is often dropped in conversation, although fuller pronunciations also occur.
The plural participle supplies the we reading in this greeting. ق is glottalized, and the attached -ak addresses a man.
As written, عمية is read as the colloquial feminine adjective blind, not the name of a language register. Colloquial Arabic is عامّية or العربية العامّية; the supplied spelling appears to be a typo.
